analysis.one_liner: Requires 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' labels on any food made with genetically engineered material or from animals fed it.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 59 cosponsors from both parties but never received a single committee vote or floor vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to sell food containing genetically engineered ingredients, or meat and poultry from animals raised on genetically engineered feed, without a prominent label saying 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED.' Companies that mislabeled food could face civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation, though small safeguards were included for farmers whose crops were accidentally mixed with engineered crops and for sellers who got written assurances from suppliers. Restaurant meals and food prepared in retail stores were exempt. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture and Commerce Committees, sent to three subcommittees, and never moved again — no hearing led to a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers who want to know whether their food contains genetically engineered ingredients, including people with allergies, religious or ethical dietary restrictions, or environmental concerns — the reasons Congress cited in the bill's findings section.

how_it_helps.text: Amends three federal food laws so that any food containing a genetically engineered material, or produced with one, is legally 'misbranded' unless it carries the required label [S2][S3].

Requires a two-part notice: the word 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' followed by a government notice that the product contains or was produced with genetically engineered material, displayed at a size comparable to nutrition facts labeling [S3].

Covers not just engineered ingredients but animals fed or injected with genetically engineered material, and processed foods containing such ingredients, so the label reaches most of the grocery aisle [S3].

The bill's findings state that consumers wish to know about engineered food for reasons including potential allergen transfer, environmental risks, and religious or ethical dietary restrictions, and that detection technology could find engineered material at levels as low as 0.1 percent [S3].

Protects farmers whose non-engineered crops are accidentally contaminated by mingling, so long as it was not intentional or negligent, and shields buyers acting in good faith on written guaranties from suppliers [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Seed and biotech companies and food manufacturers would bear the cost of testing, segregation, and relabeling products and supply chains, and some consumers might pay somewhat more as those costs were passed through. Producers feared the label would depress sales of engineered-ingredient foods.
analysis.who_pays_short: Biotech seed and packaged food companies

drawbacks.text: The mandate is extremely broad: because it covers animals merely fed engineered grain, nearly all conventional meat and poultry would have needed the label, imposing testing, segregation, and relabeling costs across the food supply that would likely be passed to shoppers [S3].

The prescribed label language is prescriptive and prominently warning-like — a large 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' notice followed by a government statement — which critics saw as stigmatizing the products rather than neutrally informing, and the bill sets the exact wording and type sizes in statute rather than leaving details to food agencies [S3].

Restaurants and ready-to-eat retail food are entirely exempt, so the same engineered ingredient would be labeled on a shelf but not in a takeout meal — an inconsistency supporters accepted to limit the bill's reach [S2][S3].

Opponents in Congress argued at the time that FDA's existing science-based review already assured safety and that mandatory labels would add costs without a health benefit; this objection did not appear in a recorded committee vote because the bill never got one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real and inexpensive per package — disclosure labeling is common in many countries — but this version was drafted broadly and prescriptively, covering animal feed and dictating exact label wording and size, which would have swept in most conventional meat and added supply-chain costs. A narrower disclosure requirement would have delivered the same information at lower cost. The bill's main flaw is scope, not purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the bill was referred to the House Agriculture and Commerce Committees and split among three subcommittees in its first week, and no subcommittee or full committee ever voted on it, so it never reached the House floor and expired when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Kucinich introduced the Genetically Engineered Food Right to Know Act in the House on November 16, 1999 [S1][S5].

It was referred to the Agriculture Committee and the Commerce Committee, and within a week split among three subcommittees: Livestock and Horticulture, Risk Management Research and Specialty Crops, and Health and Environment [S5].
The bill attracted 58 cosponsors — 54 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent — joining the sponsor [S4].

No subcommittee, committee, or floor action followed; the last recorded action is the November 30, 1999 subcommittee referral, and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies selling genetically engineered seeds and foods made with them were better off: no labeling requirement took effect, and engineered ingredients continued to go unlabeled on grocery shelves. No mandatory disclosure of engineered ingredients in the United States followed for years afterward.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was mostly Democratic — 54 Democrats, 3 Republicans, and 1 Independent signed on — but the Republican chairs who controlled the House Agriculture and Commerce Committees never allowed the bill a vote.

industries.note: A mandatory 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' label on foods made from their crops, and on meat and poultry from animals fed their grain, threatened to reduce demand and force supply-chain segregation. Their interest in avoiding the label ran against shoppers' ability to know what they were buying. Because the bill never got a vote, no labeling requirement took effect.

They would have had to verify ingredients, obtain guaranties from suppliers, and relabel products or face civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation. Compliance costs would likely have been passed to consumers in some form.

The bill exempts food served in restaurants and ready-to-eat retail food entirely [S2][S3], so they faced none of the labeling costs their grocery competitors would bear — a carve-out that locks in a two-tier disclosure system.
Clear labeling would let them distinguish their products, and the bill protects non-engineered farmers from penalties for accidental contamination by mingling [S2][S3].
